_link.title: I can explain what activation energy is and how it relates to collision theory

toLevel2.answer: The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
distractors: The energy released when products form
The total energy of the reactant particles
The average kinetic energy of the molecules

toLevel2.stem: On an energy profile diagram, activation energy is shown as the energy difference between which two points?
toLevel2.answer: The reactants and the top of the curve
distractors: The reactants and the products
The products and the top of the curve
The start and end of the reaction

toLevel2.stem: According to collision theory, what must the kinetic energy of colliding particles exceed for a reaction to occur?
distractors: The total bond energy
The enthalpy of reaction
The average particle speed

toLevel2.stem: Which symbol is commonly used to represent activation energy?
distractors: Ek
ΔH
Ep

toLevel2.stem: A reaction with a low activation energy means that:
toLevel2.answer: more particles have enough energy to react
distractors: fewer collisions occur between particles
the reaction must be endothermic
the products are at a higher energy level

toLevel2.stem: Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Every collision between reactant particles results in a chemical reaction.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: Activation energy is the {{blank:1}} energy that colliding particles must have for a {{blank:2}} to occur.
distractors: maximum
average
collision
bond

toLevel2.stem: On an energy profile diagram, activation energy is shown as the difference between the energy of the {{blank:1}} and the {{blank:2}} of the curve.
distractors: products
enthalpy
base
midpoint

toLevel2.stem: Collision theory states that particles must collide with sufficient {{blank:1}} to overcome the activation {{blank:2}}.
distractors: force
barrier
speed
state

toLevel3.stem: Why does a reaction with a high activation energy tend to proceed slowly at room temperature?
toLevel3.answer: Few particles have enough kinetic energy to overcome the energy barrier
distractors: The particles collide less frequently at lower temperatures
High activation energy makes the reaction endothermic
The particles are unable to collide at room temperature

toLevel3.stem: How does activation energy act as an energy barrier in a chemical reaction?
toLevel3.answer: It sets the minimum energy that must be reached before reactants can form products
distractors: It prevents all collisions from occurring between reactant particles
It determines the total energy change from reactants to products
It causes reactant particles to repel each other during a collision

toLevel3.stem: Two reactions occur at the same temperature. Reaction A has a lower activation energy than Reaction B. Which statement best explains why Reaction A is faster?
toLevel3.answer: A greater proportion of particles have enough energy to react in Reaction A
distractors: Particles in Reaction A move faster than those in Reaction B
Reaction A releases more energy than Reaction B
Particles in Reaction A collide more frequently than in Reaction B

toLevel3.stem: What is the relationship between the kinetic energy of colliding particles and the activation energy of a reaction?
toLevel3.answer: A collision is only successful if the kinetic energy meets or exceeds the activation energy
distractors: A collision is successful whenever any kinetic energy is present in the particles
The kinetic energy must exactly equal the activation energy for a reaction
Activation energy is the average kinetic energy of the colliding particles

toLevel3.stem: Why can two particles collide with sufficient energy but still not react?
toLevel3.answer: They may not be in the correct orientation
distractors: They may have too much kinetic energy
They may be in a closed system
They may be at different temperatures

toLevel3.stem: In terms of collision theory, what does the peak of an energy profile diagram represent?
toLevel3.answer: The transition state where bonds are partially broken and formed
distractors: The point at which the reaction releases the most heat
The average energy of all colliding particles in the system
The moment when all reactant particles have been consumed

toLevel3.stem: A reaction with a lower activation energy will have a greater proportion of successful collisions at a given temperature.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: The activation energy explains why some reactions are {{blank:1}} and others are {{blank:2}} at the same temperature.
distractors: exothermic
reversible
endothermic
spontaneous

toLevel3.stem: For a collision to be successful, particles must have sufficient {{blank:1}} and collide in the correct {{blank:2}}.
distractors: mass
temperature
speed
system

toLevel3.stem: A lower activation energy means that {{blank:1}} particles can overcome the energy {{blank:2}} at a given temperature.
distractors: fewer
level
heavier
state

toLevel4.stem: Reaction X has an activation energy of 50 kJ mol⁻¹ and Reaction Y has an activation energy of 120 kJ mol⁻¹. At room temperature, which reaction is expected to be faster and why?
toLevel4.answer: Reaction X, because more particles exceed its lower energy barrier
distractors: Reaction Y, because it has a larger energy barrier to overcome
Reaction X, because it releases more energy overall
Reaction Y, because its particles collide more frequently

toLevel4.stem: A student draws an energy profile diagram for an exothermic reaction. Where should the activation energy arrow be drawn?
toLevel4.answer: From the reactant energy level up to the peak of the curve
distractors: From the product energy level up to the peak of the curve
From the reactant energy level down to the product level
From the peak of the curve down to the product level

toLevel4.stem: In an experiment, a reaction barely proceeds at 20°C but occurs rapidly at 60°C. Using collision theory, which explanation is most accurate?
toLevel4.answer: At 60°C, more particles have kinetic energy exceeding the activation energy
distractors: At 60°C, the activation energy of the reaction decreases
At 20°C, the particles cannot collide with each other
At 60°C, the orientation requirement is eliminated

toLevel4.stem: Two gases are mixed in a container but no reaction occurs despite frequent collisions. Which collision theory factor best explains this observation?
toLevel4.answer: The particles lack sufficient energy to overcome the activation energy
distractors: The container is an open system allowing gases to escape
The particles are moving too slowly to collide with each other
The concentration of the gases is too low for any collisions

toLevel4.stem: A student observes that hydrogen peroxide decomposes very slowly without a catalyst. Using collision theory, what does this suggest about the reaction?
toLevel4.answer: It has a high activation energy so few collisions are successful
distractors: It has a low activation energy but particles rarely collide
The hydrogen peroxide molecules cannot collide at all
It has no activation energy but requires the correct orientation

toLevel4.stem: An energy profile diagram shows the reactants at 100 kJ and the peak at 180 kJ. What is the activation energy for this reaction?
distractors: 180 kJ
100 kJ
280 kJ

toLevel4.stem: A match requires striking to ignite. How does this relate to activation energy?
toLevel4.answer: Striking provides the initial energy needed to overcome the activation energy barrier
distractors: Striking reduces the activation energy of the combustion reaction
Striking increases the orientation of particles in the match head
Striking creates new reactant particles that were not previously present

toLevel4.stem: If the reactants are at 60 kJ and the peak of the energy profile is at 110 kJ, the activation energy is {{blank:1}} kJ. A reaction with a {{blank:2}} activation energy would be faster at the same temperature.
distractors: higher
equal

toLevel4.stem: When a spark ignites a fuel, the spark provides enough {{blank:1}} to overcome the {{blank:2}} energy of the combustion reaction.
distractors: heat
kinetic
force
potential

toLevel4.stem: In an experiment, Reaction P (Ea = 40 kJ mol⁻¹) is faster than Reaction Q (Ea = 95 kJ mol⁻¹) because more particles in Reaction P exceed the {{blank:1}} energy {{blank:2}}.
distractors: kinetic
level
potential
state

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that increasing temperature lowers the activation energy of a reaction. Is this claim correct?
toLevel5.answer: No — temperature increases particle energy but does not change the activation energy
distractors: Yes — higher temperature always reduces the energy barrier
Yes — heat energy is absorbed into the activation energy
No — temperature only changes the orientation of particles

toLevel5.stem: Reaction M is exothermic with a low activation energy, while Reaction N is endothermic with a high activation energy. Which statement correctly compares the two at room temperature?
toLevel5.answer: Reaction M will have a greater proportion of successful collisions than Reaction N
distractors: Reaction N will be faster because it absorbs energy from the surroundings
Both reactions will have the same rate since temperature is the same
Reaction M will be slower because exothermic reactions are always slow

toLevel5.stem: Two students debate why a particular reaction is slow. Student A says the activation energy is high. Student B says the particles rarely collide in the correct orientation. Which student could be correct?
toLevel5.answer: Either student — both high Ea and poor orientation reduce successful collisions
distractors: Only Student A — orientation has no effect on reaction rate
Only Student B — activation energy does not affect reaction rate
Neither student — slow reactions are caused only by low concentration

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'If we remove the activation energy barrier entirely, every collision would result in a reaction.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — particles must still collide in the correct orientation
distractors: Correct — energy is the only requirement for a reaction
Incorrect — particles must also be in a closed system
Correct — orientation only matters when Ea is high

toLevel5.stem: An energy profile diagram shows that the activation energy for the forward reaction is 80 kJ mol⁻¹ and the overall energy change is −50 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy for the reverse reaction?
distractors: 80 kJ mol⁻¹
50 kJ mol⁻¹
30 kJ mol⁻¹

toLevel5.stem: A peer claims that two reactions with the same activation energy must proceed at the same rate. Is this a valid conclusion?
toLevel5.answer: No — rate also depends on collision frequency and particle orientation
distractors: Yes — activation energy is the only factor that determines rate
No — rate depends only on whether the system is open or closed
Yes — equal activation energy guarantees equal reaction rates

toLevel5.stem: In a mixture of three different reactions occurring simultaneously, Reaction A has the lowest activation energy. Which conclusion is best supported?
toLevel5.answer: Reaction A is most likely to have the greatest proportion of successful collisions
distractors: Reaction A will definitely finish first regardless of other conditions
Reaction A must be exothermic since it has the lowest activation energy
Reaction A will not occur if the other reactions consume all the energy

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that activation energy is irrelevant for exothermic reactions because they release energy. Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — all reactions must overcome their activation energy before any energy is released
distractors: Correct — exothermic reactions provide their own activation energy
Incorrect — exothermic reactions have no activation energy at all
Correct — the energy released drives the reaction without any barrier

toLevel5.stem: Increasing temperature does not change the {{blank:1}} energy but increases the proportion of particles with sufficient energy to {{blank:2}} it.
distractors: kinetic
match
potential
absorb

toLevel5.stem: Two reactions with identical activation energies can have different rates because rate also depends on collision {{blank:1}} and particle {{blank:2}}.
distractors: energy
temperature
mass
volume
